pr_title: Handle sigchld instead of blocking on waitpid
pr_body:
This stops any potential blocking when killing swaybg (e.g. reloading config). We also forcefully close their wayland connection, in case they're slow to die and we start a new swaybg.

This fixes an issue that was reported by someone on IRC, but doesn't have a github issue.

Fixes #2952
pr_comments:
Looking into this further, I think this now needs a more elaborate solution than what's here. Basically, we need to make sure we don't reap children from other places, such as a direct-session or xwayland in wlroots.
The most obvious way would be to create a process group and put all of the processes we want to watch in there. Then it becomes `waitpid(-pgid, NULL, WNOHANG)`.
If we do file-descriptor handling too (instead of pids), then this basically turns into a service manager and possibly the foundation of privileged clients.

Well, if all we care about is swaybg, we can just start it in a double-fork so we don't care about reaping (and just need to waitpid at start time); but that has the same problem we currently have is that we're killing a pid we have no idea if that still is swaybg.
If on top of that we don't kill at all but just destroy the wayland client like you do here (need some message passing on double-fork to identify the right one but we do that in sway exec anyway), that solves both problem without the need for a full blown manager. I just checked, destroying the client makes swaybg exit.
(EDIT: there's still the possibility that another process took the same pid and is a wayland client so we'd destroy the wrong client, I guess that cannot be solved without such a manager, but it's not a new problem - not sure how much we care about that)

EDIT2: note to self, recompile when you test something -- I take what I just wrote back, destroying the wayland client doesn't make swaybg stop, need to look into why

EDIT3: actually it does die, we just start two swaybg too close to each other when reloading config (I have output foo + output * so reloading restarts swaybg twice), and the first one hasn't finished connecting to the wayland socket yet when we try to kill it, so it doesn't get terminated by closing the wayland connection because it's not connected yet... Then it stays forever.
I think we could fix that by just reloading the output config once per output per reload, but I guess it's still not as reliable as a real service manager.

issue_context.title: Configuration reload leaves orphaned swaybg processes
issue_context.body:
After reloading my configuration, I am seeing some orphaned swaybg processes hanging about. In fact each reload generates two of them.

I am running Void Linux, glibc, kernel 4.18.16, with elogind.

Please tell me if there is any more information you need.
comments:
I could not reproduce your issue, could you post your configuration?
Alternatively you can try to reproduce with the default config file.
I can reproduce with the default configuration.
Please provide a debug log and the exact sway version. (see https://github.com/swaywm/sway/wiki#how-do-i-report-issues)
Hmm, just realized I still have swaybar processes left behind when I Ctrl+C sway.
Is anyone still able to replicate this?
FWIW I have not seen this exact behavior, but I did see a zombie swaybg recently.
I'm going to close this, as we now disconnect swaybg instead of killing it.

review_comments: `swaybg` can be set to a third-party client, e.g. oguri. This client can open multiple connections. We shouldn't break here.
`wl_client_get_credentials` can fail (e.g. on FreeBSD where it's not supported). We should either check the return value or initialize `p` to 0 to make sure we don't kill random clients.

Looking at the freebsd patches for libwayland, it will simply set the pid to 0, which won't break the logic of this loop; it just won't close the connection.

wl_client_get_credentials has no return value. It's just a getter for values which are read right when the client connects.

The only other way I can think to track this is through the socket file descriptor. It would require us opening it ourselves and using WAYLAND_SOCKET, and would require a fair bit of reworking. Not to mention it doesn't work if a process wants multiple connections (do we want to allow that?).
Checking for the pid seems like to most reliable way, at least for Linux.

>wl_client_get_credentials has no return value

Oh, all right then, I somehow had the feeling it could fail but I've mixed things up.
similarily I think this should match against known pids (e.g. swaybg_pid etc) and unset the values if it died, so we don't kill a random process later if a user killed swaybg themselves.

I would also do the kill before `wl_client_destroy` (before the whole loop?).
If a well-behaved client notices the destroy (that closes the socket connection right?) and exits before we send the kill, it's possible that the pid gets reused meanwhile which would make us kill a random process, or in most cases we could log an error.
